subtitle: Three quantities, one equation, and a great deal of engineering that follows from it. Every circuit in these notes runs, so you will watch the law work before you ever write it down.

intro.body:
Let’s begin with a garden hose. Open the tap a little and a trickle comes out; open it fully and it gushes; pinch the hose and the flow drops. You already understand, in your hands, everything this lesson is about. We are just going to give the three characters proper names.

Voltage (V, in volts) is the electrical pressure a source applies, the push behind the water. Current (I, in amperes) is the rate of charge flow that results, the water actually moving. Resistance (R, in ohms) is how strongly a component opposes that flow, the pinch in the hose.

Here is how we will work. We build a real circuit, measure it, test a prediction against it, and only then state the law that connects the three. The measurement comes first deliberately: an equation whose behaviour you have already watched is a very different object from one handed to you cold.

How to read these notesEvery circuit here is live. Each one carries its own Simulate button: press it and the solver runs that circuit, the meters start reading, and the sliders under it change the circuit while it runs. Nothing is a picture of a result — it is the result. Press Reset to put a circuit back as drawn.
Before you start. Nothing here is timed and nothing is scored. Answering a question wrong routes you to the reason that answer is tempting, and then shows you the circuit that settles it. Select any sentence you find unclear and choose Ask about this to put that exact wording in front of the assistant.
keynotes: Voltage (V, volts) is the electrical pressure, current (I, amperes) is the resulting rate of charge flow, and resistance (R, ohms) is how strongly a component opposes it.
These notes measure first and state the law afterwards.
Every circuit is live: press Simulate, use the sliders, and Reset to restore it.

circuit.body:
Time to build the smallest complete circuit there is: a voltage source and a single resistor joined in a loop. The source holds a fixed potential difference across its terminals, and the resistor is the only thing limiting how much current flows. Think of a pump pushing water round a closed pipe with one narrow section.

Here a 9 V battery drives a 330 Ω resistor, and we have attached two instruments. Notice how they are wired, because this is where beginners trip. The ammeter goes in series: the loop passes through it, so it reads the current flowing round. The voltmeter goes in parallel with the resistor, across it and not through it, so it reads the potential difference between the resistor’s two ends.

Those two placements are not interchangeable, and getting them the wrong way round is the first mistake most people make with a real meter. (A neat way to remember it: you measure how fast the river flows by standing in it, but you measure the height of a waterfall by looking across it.) Press Simulate and watch the meters settle.
circuit.after: Two numbers, read off two instruments: 27.3 mA and 9.00 V. Everything that follows is an attempt to predict numbers like these before measuring them. Can you see why 9.00 V is the whole battery voltage? There is only one resistor to spend it on.
keynotes: The simplest circuit is a voltage source and one resistor in a loop; the resistor alone limits the current.
A 9 V battery across 330 Ω gives an ammeter reading of 27.3 mA and a voltmeter reading of 9.00 V.
An ammeter goes in series (the loop passes through it); a voltmeter goes in parallel (across the component).

predict.body:
Now comes the part I like best. Before any equation, I want you to bet. Two predictions, each changing exactly one thing about Figure 2.1, each asking what the ammeter will do.

Commit to an answer before reading on. Being wrong here is the most useful thing that can happen in this lesson, because it is the fastest way to find out what you actually believe as opposed to what you can recite. And don’t worry: nothing is scored. Each answer is followed by the circuit that settles it, which you can run yourself.
keynotes: Predict first: commit to an answer before looking, because being wrong teaches the most.
Each prediction changes exactly one thing about Figure 2.1: the resistance, or the supply.
Every answer is followed by a circuit you can run to settle it.

measure.body:
Two points might be a coincidence. A pattern needs a sweep. So let’s try five common resistor values on the same 9 V source and see what the current does. The table below lists the current each one draws, with the power it dissipates alongside, and the chart plots the same data.

Read the table carefullyLook at 100 Ω and 1000 Ω — a factor of ten in resistance. The current falls from 90 mA to 9 mA, also a factor of ten. Every row obeys the same ratio.

Did you spot it? Multiply the resistance by ten and the current shrinks to a tenth. That is an inverse relationship, and the curve in the second figure shows what it looks like: steep at the left, flattening toward the right as the resistance climbs. And notice the power column too. Because power depends on both current and voltage, a tenth of the current means a tenth of the power as well.
keynotes: At a fixed 9 V, ten times the resistance gives one tenth the current: 100 Ω draws 90 mA and 1000 Ω draws 9 mA.
Power also falls to a tenth, because it depends on both current and voltage.
Current plotted against resistance is a curve that flattens toward the right: an inverse relationship.

law.body:
What you measured has a name, and it comes from a schoolteacher. In 1827 Georg Ohm published the result that, for a conductor at constant temperature, the current through it is directly proportional to the voltage across it and inversely proportional to its resistance. Read that sentence twice. Both halves are things you have now watched happen with your own eyes.

Now let’s write it down, one step at a time. Each line below is the same idea in a different arrangement, and each arrangement answers a different question.
law.after:
A law with conditions. Ohm's law is not universal — it describes ohmic materials, those whose resistance stays constant as voltage changes. A filament lamp heats up and its resistance rises; a diode conducts in one direction only. Both are non-ohmic, and both appear in §11.

Hold on to that warning. It will save you from a classic trap later on.
keynotes: Ohm’s law (1827): current is directly proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance, I = V/R.
Rearranged: V = IR for tracking voltages round a loop, and R = V/I as the measurement form a multimeter uses.
Power is P = VI = I²R = V²/R, so doubling the supply quadruples the heat in a resistor.
The law describes ohmic materials, whose resistance stays constant; a filament lamp and a diode are non-ohmic.

worked-basic.body:
Let’s put numbers through the law together. A 9.0 V supply is connected across a 330 Ω resistor. Find the current through it and the power it dissipates.

Each step is revealed one at a time. Attempt it yourself before opening the next. Seriously, try it: the moment you struggle is the moment you learn.

Spoiler, so you can check yourself as you go: the current comes out as 0.02727 A (27.3 mA) and the power as 0.245 W.
keynotes: Choose the form that has the unknown alone: I = V/R when voltage and resistance are known.
9.0 V across 330 Ω gives I = 0.02727 A = 27.3 mA, and the units confirm the arrangement.
Power P = VI = 0.245 W, which matches the wattmeter’s 245.5 mW; a 0.25 W resistor would be at its limit, so choose a 0.5 W part.

series.body:
One resistor is lonely. What happens when you put two end to end? Think of two narrow sections in the same hose: all the water must pass through both, because there is nowhere else for it to go. So the same current passes through each, and their resistances simply add. The pair behaves as one resistor of the combined value.

Try it with 220 Ω and 330 Ω in series across 9 V. The total is 550 Ω, so the current is 16.4 mA. And here is the lovely part: each resistor takes a share of the supply voltage in proportion to its own resistance, 3.60 V across the 220 Ω and 5.40 V across the 330 Ω. The two shares sum to 9.00 V, which is Kirchhoff’s voltage law arriving a lesson early.

Press Simulate and check that the ammeter reads one current for the whole loop while the two voltmeters show the two shares.
series.after: This arrangement is a potential divider, and it is one of the most used circuits in electronics: two resistors turn a supply voltage into any smaller voltage you choose. Keep it in your toolbox; you will meet it everywhere.
keynotes: In series the same current flows through every resistor, and the resistances add.
220 Ω and 330 Ω in series across 9 V total 550 Ω and carry 16.4 mA.
Each resistor takes a share of the supply proportional to its resistance: 3.60 V and 5.40 V, summing to 9.00 V.
Two resistors in series form a potential divider.

worked-series.body:
Let’s do the divider properly, step by step. A 9.0 V supply is connected across 220 Ω and 330 Ω in series. Find the current and the voltage across each resistor. Cover the steps, make your own attempt, then compare.

The numbers to aim for: 550 Ω in total, a loop current of 16.4 mA, then 3.60 V and 5.40 V across the two resistors.
keynotes: Combine the resistances first: 220 + 330 = 550 Ω.
The loop current is 9.0/550 = 16.4 mA, the same everywhere in the loop.
Apply V = IR to each resistor: 3.60 V across the 220 Ω and 5.40 V across the 330 Ω.
Check the shares add to the supply: 3.60 + 5.40 = 9.00 V.

parallel.body:
There is another way to connect two resistors, and it behaves almost like the opposite. Connect them across the same pair of nodes and they are in parallel. Picture two pipes branching from the same tank. Now the shared quantity is voltage, not current: both resistors have the full supply across them, and each draws whatever current Ohm’s law gives it, independently of the other. The currents then add.

This surprises people the first time. Adding a second path can only add current, so the total resistance of a parallel pair is always less than the smaller of the two. Add a second checkout lane and the queue moves faster, never slower.

Press Simulate with 220 Ω and 330 Ω across the supply and you will see you can predict every meter: the branches read 40.9 mA and 27.3 mA, and the supply meter reads their sum, 68.2 mA. Each branch takes exactly what it would take alone. Then work through the derivation below, and notice how neatly the reciprocals fall out.
parallel.after: The equivalent resistance of Figure 9.1 is Rp = (220 × 330)/(220 + 330) = 132 Ω, and 9 / 132 = 68.2 mA — the number on the supply ammeter. Working from either end gives the same answer, which is the usual sign that the model is consistent rather than a coincidence.
keynotes: In parallel the voltage is common and the branch currents add.
Reciprocals add, so for two resistors the combination is their product over their sum, always smaller than the smaller resistor.
For 220 Ω and 330 Ω in parallel across 9 V the branches carry 40.9 mA and 27.3 mA, and the supply delivers 68.2 mA.
The equivalent resistance is 132 Ω, and 9/132 gives the same 68.2 mA.

power.body:
Here is a fact of life: every resistor turns the energy it takes out of the circuit into heat. Touch a resistor that has been working hard and you will feel it. How much heat? That is the power, P = VI, and substituting Ohm’s law gives two forms that are usually more convenient: P = I²R when you know the current, P = V²/R when you know the voltage.

The V² is the part worth tattooing on your memory. Power does not rise in proportion to voltage; it rises with the square of it. Double a supply and the heat in a fixed resistor goes up four times. Take the 330 Ω resistor dissipating 0.245 W at 9 V: at 18 V it must cope with four times that. A component that was comfortable at 9 V is at four times its dissipation at 18 V, which is how most resistors actually die.

Press Simulate and drag the supply slider. The current tracks the voltage in a straight line, but the power does not: it climbs far faster at the top of the range than at the bottom.
keynotes: Every resistor turns the energy it takes into heat: P = VI, or P = I²R when current is known and P = V²/R when voltage is.
Power rises with the square of voltage: doubling the supply quadruples the heat in a fixed resistor.
The 330 Ω resistor dissipating 0.245 W at 9 V is at four times that at 18 V, which is how most resistors die.

nonohmic.body:
Remember the warning about conditions? Here is where it bites. Ohm’s law describes components with a constant R. Plenty of useful components do not have one, and treating them as though they did produces answers that are wrong in a way the arithmetic cannot reveal.

A light-emitting diode is the clearest case. It conducts in one direction only, and once it conducts it holds a roughly fixed voltage across itself, about 2 V for a red LED, almost regardless of the current. It has no meaningful resistance: ask for V/I and you get a different answer at every current.

This is why an LED is always driven through a series resistor. The resistor is the ohmic part, and it is what sets the current; the LED simply takes its 2 V and lights. Look at the figure at the fork: the question is not what a part is made of, but whether its resistance stays put while the voltage changes.

Then try the lamp. Press Simulate: 450 mA through a 20 Ω lamp, and it glows. Drag the switch slider to 0 while it runs and the lamp goes out, because an open switch is a resistance so large that no useful current crosses it.
nonohmic.after: The lamp is idealised here. This model gives the filament a fixed 20 Ω. A real filament is several times more resistive when hot than when cold, so switching one on draws a large inrush current for a few milliseconds — which is why filament lamps almost always fail at the moment they are switched on rather than during use.
keynotes: Ohm’s law needs a constant R; components without one, like an LED, break the arithmetic.
A red LED holds roughly 2 V across itself once it conducts, almost regardless of current.
An LED is always driven through a series resistor, which is the ohmic part that sets the current.
The lamp passes 450 mA through 20 Ω, and an open switch is a resistance so large that no useful current crosses it.

misuse.body:
Ohm’s law is simple enough that the errors rarely come from the algebra; they come from misapplying it. I have watched these three trip up students, and engineers, for years, so let’s name them now and take the sting out of them.

The figure shows the order to work any DC circuit problem. The two decisions in it are exactly where the mistakes below happen: combining before finding the loop current, and taking V from the supply instead of from the component. Read the three traps, and ask yourself honestly which one you are most likely to fall into.
keynotes: Convert to volts, amperes and ohms first: using milliamperes or kilohms directly gives answers wrong by a factor of a thousand.
V in I = V/R is the voltage across that resistor, not the supply voltage.
A single R does not describe a lamp filament, a diode or a thermistor; the result holds only at one operating point.

problems.body: Now it is your turn. Seven problems over everything above. Work each one on paper before opening its answer, because the answer is worth very little if you have not first been wrong about something. Where a problem can be settled by measurement, its answer carries the circuit that settles it: press Simulate and read the instrument. Take your time; nobody is watching the clock.
keynotes: Work every problem on paper before opening its answer.
Where a problem can be settled by measurement, its answer carries a circuit: press Simulate and read the instrument.
There are seven problems, covering everything in the lesson.

summary.body:
Look at what you did. You predicted, measured, derived and calculated, in that order, and every number you were given came off an instrument you can run yourself. That is how engineers actually learn a law, and it is why the numbers now feel like yours rather than the textbook’s. If any one of the six statements below feels slippery, go back and rerun its circuit. The lesson reduces to six statements.

  1. Ohm's law is I = V/R, rearranged as V = IR or R = V/I as the problem requires.
  2. Current is proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance — halving the supply and doubling the resistance produce the identical 13.6 mA.
  3. Power is P = VI = I²R = V²/R, it rises with the square of voltage, and it decides which physical component you can actually use.
  4. Series resistances add, the current is common, and each resistor takes a share of the supply in proportion to its own value.
  5. Parallel resistances combine reciprocally, the voltage is common, and the branch currents add — so a parallel pair is always easier to drive than either part alone.
  6. The law describes ohmic components only. An LED holds its forward voltage and a filament changes with temperature; for these, the resistor beside them is what the law is applied to.
Next in this courseLesson 2 — Kirchhoff's laws: what happens once a circuit has more than one loop and current has somewhere else to go. The two rules you have already used informally here — shares around a loop sum to the supply, branch currents sum at a junction — are exactly the two laws, stated properly.
keynotes: I = V/R, rearranged as V = IR or R = V/I as the problem needs.
Series resistances add with a common current; parallel resistances combine reciprocally with a common voltage.
Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R rises with the square of voltage and decides which physical component you can use.
Ohm’s law applies to ohmic components only; next comes Kirchhoff’s laws for circuits with more than one loop.
